strengths: The composite-priority construction is simple and well motivated. The tier-size and harmonic-ancestor arguments provide a convincing route to an O(1 + log(1/w_x)) expected-depth bound for arbitrary fixed weights, addressing the limitations of deterministic frequency priorities.

The static analysis gives a useful connection between prediction quality and search cost through cross entropy: O(m[1 + H(p) + D_KL(p||q)]). The adversarial constructions also help explain why alternative priority assignments can perform poorly.

The working-set score is an interesting component: its total weight is bounded, and it changes only for the accessed key. This provides a potentially useful connection between frequency-sensitive trees and temporal locality, although the maintenance guarantees require correction.
weaknesses: The weight-update guarantee in Corollary 2.7 is false as stated. Take n = 2^(2^k), give every other key weight 1/(2n), and change one key's weight from (1-epsilon)/n to (1+epsilon)/n. Initially all keys occupy the same tier; afterward the changed key occupies a higher-priority tier and becomes the root. This requires Theta(log n) expected rotations, although |log(w'/w)| tends to zero. Moreover, C.2's deletion-and-reinsertion argument yields a sum of logarithmic costs, not the claimed logarithm of a ratio. Consequently, the subsequent analyses that charge updates to logarithmic weight variation are unsupported.

The B-tree construction does not handle negative tiers, undermining a principal extension. In C.2, different tiers occupy separate blocks, but the depth analysis sums only over nonnegative tiers. For B = 2^(2^r), ordered keys with weights w_j = 2^(-2^j), j = 0,...,r-1, have distinct negative tiers and total weight below one. The construction creates a chain of r blocks, although the last key has log_B(1/w_j) = 1/2. Additional low-weight keys can satisfy the stated relationship between n and B. An explicit treatment of these tiers is necessary.

Several robustness claims exceed what is proved. Theorem 2.13 establishes an upper bound through cross entropy; it does not establish that actual additional cost equals m times KL divergence. Similarly, D.2 substitutes an upper bound for cost(X,w) into an actual-cost comparison without justification. Separately, C.6 uses a lower bound on the true probability as though it also bounded the predicted probability away from zero. The stated distance condition does not imply this, leaving C.6 and its dependent corollaries unsupported without smoothing or additional assumptions.

The experiments contain discrepancies that prevent confident interpretation. Under the stated exact uniform weights, every key receives the same tier, so the proposed tree has exactly the distribution of a standard randomized treap; Figure 4 nevertheless reports a substantial performance gap. This requires reconciliation with the implementation or a precise explanation of whether realized sample frequencies are used. Figure 5 also shows substantial changes in prediction-independent baselines as KL divergence varies. The paper must clarify whether the true workload is held fixed; otherwise this experiment does not isolate prediction error. These issues are more consequential than the inconsistent descriptions of the horizontal axes.

The contribution needs clearer positioning against classical weighted randomized search trees and weighted treaps, which already provide frequency-sensitive expected search depths. The paper discusses classical optimal BSTs but does not adequately explain what composite bucketing gains over these alternatives or include a corresponding baseline. A well-motivated alternative construction can be valuable, but the significance of the surviving static result remains insufficiently established given the problems with the dynamic and external-memory extensions.
